Resolution concerning advances to the King's Printer to enable him to make purchases and to pay wages to workmen, reported ; read the second time, and agreed to.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 137) an Act to amend the Act respecting the Department of Public Printing and Stationery.
Explain ?

I will be glad to repeat the explanation I gave the other day. We propose to give legal authority to a practice which has long prevailed in this department with regard to the funds necessary for carrying on the work. We have supplied a thoroughly equipped printing establishment, but we supplied no working capital. The King's Printer receives his money from parliament and from the various departments, but while he is waiting for that, as any ordinary business man must wait for the returns of his customers, he has to pay for supplies and wages. Hitherto he has received a credit for that purpose from the Auditor General, but attention has been drawn to the fact that there is no legal authority for that practice and this Bill legalizes it.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time, and agreed to.

speechtext: I am pleased .to see the minister recognizing the rights of a number of the officers who have been retired during recent years. As the minister knows, some officers were retired recently at the age of sixty years, when under the "law I think they might have held on until they were sixty-two or sixty-three. These men would have been subject to the terms and

conditions of this Pension Bill if they had not been so retired. I would again urge on the government the very great importance and the fairness of providing for these men. I believe that those who are more able, from their military experience, to speak on this subject than I am, are unanimous in their desire to have this done, and I am sure that the government in doing so will have the unanimous support at any rate of this side of the House. It appears to me that those men who have devoted the best part of their lives to the service of their country, with all the risks incident to their calling, have a specially strong claim upon the government. All other governments are most liberal in their treatment of men who have devoted themselves to the defence of their country. I have received a letter from a commission merchant complaining of the bill, and suggesting that It should be amended to read ' every basket of fruit sold to consumers in Canada.' It would then not affect the wholesale or commission men. but would affect only those who sell direct to consumers. My correspondent says that the profit is so small that the trade will be injured by the expense involved if the Bill interferes with the wholesale men.
The result of that would be to allow the commission man to unload on the retailer a lot of baskets which it would be illegal to sell.
They buy in bulk.

The commission man simply acts as the agent of the producer, and would not be responsible.

We beg to state that the Winnipeg Produce Exchange are satisfied that the Bill is all right as far as Canadian small fruits are concerned. size of basket for strawberries. Or at any place before it is sold to the consumer ?
No. If any one has a complaint, and lays it before the proper officer, the inspector, or the deputy inspector of weights and measures, will have an inspection made.
It is my opinion that the proper thing to do would be to inspect the twine at the place where it is manufactured, and in the case of imported American twine, it should be inspected while in bond.

The previous clauses of this Bill were incorporated last year in the Bill presented by the then hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Frost), who, I understand, is a practical man, being a farm implement manufacturer, and also an importer and seller of a large quantity of binder twine. The effect of the law cannot yet be determined, because the Bill only came into effect last October. When the Bill was introduced the idea was to protect the farmer against being imposed upon in buying twine which was not of the length represented. My hon. friend (Mr. Stephens) will see that it is impossible to inspect the twine at the place of manufacture. We do not exclude binder twine imported from the United States, and it would not seem possible that a Canadian officer could cross the line and inspect binder twine in the United States factories. There are two provisions in the Bill : one which imposes a penalty on the party who neglects to put a stamp on the ball, and the other providing a penalty on the manufacturer or importer of binder twine when the correct length as required by law is not stamped on the ball.

After careful examination we tliouglit that, for the present at least, this was the only way of protecting the" farmer against these frauds in the selling of binder twine.

This twine should be inspected in the bags. After a bag of twine is emptied out it is open to any person to change the tags, but if the bag were opened and that twine inspected in the bags, then I think some of this danger would be avoided. After the bags are opened and the twine taken out, it is very easy for a person so disposed to change the tags and then make a complaint that the twine is not right, and thus get an innocent person into trouble. It would avoid a great deal of difficulty if the twine were inspected in the bags.

It seems to me that that would make it utterly impossible to have a proper inspection at all. The Bill provides that Canadian manufacturers must put a stamp on each ball, and the length of feet in it. That is a protection against our own manufacturers, and if the United States manufacturers hope to capture the Canadian trade they must comply with all the conditions that our people have to comply with. My hon. friend (Mr. Stephens) is a practical hardware man, but he seems to anticipate some difficulties that are not likely to arise. It would be bordering on folly for a man who purchases twine, and is glad to have the number of feet he pays for, to change the tag, and then make a complaint against the seller for the mere sake of having him fined. I do not think we need be in the least alarmed about that. My hon. friend for Kent knows perfectly well that it would be impossible to attempt to inspect all the twine in bags. We must cast the responsibility upon the manufacturer and the seller rather than upon our officers, by asking them to do work which it is impossible for them to do. My hon. friend (Mr. Stephens) will find that the Bill is quite workable, and that his objection is not so serious as he anticipates.

Before whom is this information to be laid against the manufacturer and importer ? Must it be done with the consent of the' inspector of weights and measures in a particular locality, or can it be done before any justice of the peace ?

If the purchaser thinks that the ball of twine which has been sold to him does not contain the proper quantity, he may apply to any weights and measures inspector and get a certificate, that after inspection there was a deficiency in the length of the twine.

Why should he not go directly to a justice of the peace and lay an information in the ordinary way for an infringement of the law? Otherwise the enforcement of the law would be very clumsy.
I see nothing in the Act which compels the complainant to apply to the inspector of weights and measures. To my mind, the procedure would be very simple. If you find a ball of twine without a tag, the maker is liable to a penalty of twenty-five cents for each ball, and if the length is not stamped on that tag, he is liable to a penalty of from $1 to $25. I would think that an aggrieved person should be allowed to lay an information before a magistrate in the ordinary way and have the case tried. I think this Act affords a splendid protection [DOT] to the agriculturists of this country, for I have no doubt that in many instances, particularly in the case of imported twine, they have been imposed upon.	-

I completely agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) that this is a very good law if it can be made workable. If a man goes out in the country and opens a bag of twine he may have another tag in his pocket, and he may be disposed to place that other tag on the ball, The twine is 650 feet long, we will say, and he would put on a tag saying it was 450 feet long, and then he might go around and say it was not the proper length. He takes that ball of twine to a magistrate and has the man who sold it to him fined. It is not the fine that the merchant dislikes ; it is the disgrace to his business. If it is found that he sold a ball of twine supposed to run GSR feet to the pound, and it only measured 45R feet, people would say that he was dishonest in all his transactions. I think all the dangers which the hon. member for Kent is suggesting are imaginary. He knows perfectly well that such a thing could not happen, for this reason. The ball of twine measuring 650 feet is pure manlla, and is stamped as such. Even without the stamp a ball of pure sisal could not be mistaken for manila ; and if somebody transferred the stamp from one to the other, anybody could detect it at once. There is no possibility of the danger which the hon. member for Kent suggests. I think it is an admirable proposal that every ball of twine, whether imported or manufactured in Canada, should be stamped with the length per pound. If one dealer sells at 10 cents a pound and another at 121 cents, the purchaser can easily reckon which is the cheaper, for if the 10-cent twine is 450 feet to the pound and the 121-cent twine 650 feet, the latter is the cheaper, and the purchaser knows exactly what he is doing. It is a protection to the purchaser and the honest dealer. There cannot be a transference of the tag. Suppose a dishonest man wanted to do so, where would he get the tag ? He could only transfer a tag from one ball to another, and he would be no gainer by doing tiiat. because if he put a manila tag on a ball of sisal, he would only disclose the dishonesty of the

transaction. There is no danger in the proposal at all.

There is a large cordage factory at Dartmouth which manufactures a lot of this twine, and it goes west. Suppose that two or three of these tags were dropped off in transit, what is to he done in that case ?

The balls are all put up in bags, and the tags cannot drop off.
. Mr. STEPHENS. The hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) says one can easily detect the difference between one kind of twine and another. The difference has only to be 5 per cent to make a man liable. One ' could not tell a difference of 10 per cent unless he is a good expert, and it is very doubtful if even an expert could tell it. With regard to changing the tags, the hon. gentleman asks, where would you get the tags ? The country is full of tags in harvest time, and there would be no trouble in getting them. The reason I asked before whom the information could be laid and at whose instance, is that a difficulty might arise between rival manufacturers. The skill necessary to detect frauds of the kind aimed at is not the possession of the users of binder twine, and it is very easy for a rival manufacturer to destroy the reputation of another. You cannot tell the twine of one manufacturer from that of another ; you cannot tell a 500-foot ball from a GOO-foot ball ; it requires an expert to do so. I look forward with considerable satisfaction to the fact that this law will give the farmers a chance. At the same [DOT]time, its application is surrounded by a great deal of difficulty. To give any one power to lodge a complaint against a manufacturer or a merchant without a thorough inspection by the inspector of weights and measures, would render a man liable to have his reputation as an honest manufacturer or dealer destroyed at the instigation of a business rival. It is easy to put a GOO-foot Mr. WALLACE.
tag on a 050-foot ball ; and the only way to protect the manufacturers and the dealers is to see that the power to lay an information before a justice of the peace is not in the hands of everybody.
What provision makes it necessary that there should be a certificate from the inspector of weights and measures before a prosecution can be commenced ?

There is no such provision in the Act. If a man charges another with having taken a stamp from one ball and put it on another, the burden of proof falls upon him. If he wants to have the guilty party punished he had better apply to an inspector of weights and measures in order to secure evidence that the ball was opened and measured in the presence of a public officer. Another witness might do the same thing. But there is no provision in the law which compels a man to apply to the officers of the department. He may go before the magistrate and make his case good, if possible.

I want to make it clear to the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) that there is no necessity of procuring a certificate before a prosecution is commenced. It is perfectly clear, as the minister says, that the burden of proving the offence is on the prosecutor. There may be some difficulty, such as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Kent in this respect, that as the facts upon which the transaction depends may in such a case exist only in the knowledge of the prosecutor, and not at all in the knowledge of the defendant, the defendant is to a certain extent at the mercy of the prosecutor. That, however, is not peculiar to this particular provision. It exists with regard to a great many cases under the law, and I suppose the result would be to make a justice of the peace, or any other tribunal before whom a case of this kind is brought, more careful to weigh the evidence and more earnest in seeing that the evidence of the prosecutor is confirmed by other evidence as to which there can be no doubt. But so far as the necessity for any certificate is concerned, that does not exist under the law. Any person can swear that a particular tag was on the ball, or, without producing the ball at all. he may swear that he used it and found it deficient. If he should do what 1 have just suggested, it might discredit his evidence, but it would be perfectly competent for him to attempt it. I desire to make this statement so that there will be no misunderstanding as to the effect of the provision.

I quite appreciate the position taken by the hon. member for Kent. The tendency of all

these laws seems at first to harass and embarrass the trader, but in the Revenue Department we have similar laws governing the sales of many commodities of life, such as spices, baking powder, coal oil, tobacco, and all the ordinary things that enter into the grocery business, and even some articles of dry goods. I think it a very good precaution that the length of the cord in a ball of binder twine should be stamped upon the ball by the manufacturer, and that he should be made responsible just as is the man who puts his stamp on a barrel of apples. It should be made imperative on the manufacturers to supply the farmers exactly with the quantity of binder twine they pay for. I am glad to know that it is not in the province of any one to bring an ordinary trader before a justice of the peace for every small infraction of the law, but that the law shall be administered by the Department of Inland Revenue.
That is not the case.

The clause provides that any proceeding under this section shall be taken within six months from the sale of any such balls. When you do not provide that the proceedings shall he before a justice of the peace, are they not to be instituted by the Department of Inland Revenue ?
No.
However, I am quite in favour of the Bill. Let us make it a workable one, which will protect the farmers in connection with the binder twine business.
I would have binder twine inspected the same ns coal oil is. Coal oil is inspected in the full barrel, and binder twine should be inspected in the full bag.

Hon. gentlemen lose sight of the fact that the penalty is not on account of a certain number of feet not being in the ball, but a certain number of pounds. The law requires that the twine should measure a certain number of feet per pound, and not per ball.
Every one understands that.

Therefore, I fail to see the difficulty which the hon. gentleman anticipates. A manufacturer would possibly not make more than three or four qualities in any season, and would simply have three or four tags. Say he makes four brands of twine, he would have four different tags, so that there would be no difficulty in mixing up the balls or in determining whether a tag has been removed from one ball or another. Any man who is a judge could determine whether the
article is pure manila or pure sisal, or an admixture of the two.
If a man takes a pound of pure manila twine and finds it does not measure 600 feet, or such length as the tag indicates, the factory is liable to a penalty of from $1 to $25 for infringement of the law.
I do not see any danger of getting tags from different balls confused one with another, because we could simply refer to another ball of the same quality or to the manufacturer himself to ascertain what length of twine was in each pound. To my mind, the law as now proposed is very simple, and I hope it will be very effective.

The committee must not lose sight of the fact that this clause was passed at the last session of parliament, and the manufacturers are complying with its terms. It should not be the desire of this parliament to change the law when the manufacturers are actually engaged in complying with it. Surely it is in the public interest that this law, which was fully discussed last year and went into operation last October, should be given a year's, trial before changing it.

I would like to ask the hon. minister in what manner he proposes to have this law put into effect. Who shall be the examiners, the inspectors of weights and measures of the counties or private individuals ? It will be very difficult for a farmer to measure a ball of twine to ascertain its length to the pound, in fact, he almost spoils the ball for his use when he unwinds it, for he cannot get it back into its original shape again. I think inspectors of weights and measures should be instructed to examine the different brands of twine when they come into the country. And, of course, if it is known by the manufacturers that the inspector of weights and measures will be on the watch, they will be careful not to infringe on the law.

The enactment of the law will have the effect upon the manufacturers of compelling them to make the twine the right length. But the difficulty is that a manufacturer may be unjustifiably condemned through a rival manufacturer falsifying the amount of twine in a ball. That is the only objection I have heard. On such a basis, a manufacturer may be fined by a justice of the peace, and rival manufacturers will advertise throughout the length and breadth of the country that this man has been fined for selling short twine. I do not believe there is a manufacturer in Canada who would offer twine shorter than the standard.

Then, what is the trouble ?
Mr. KEY'D. There is no trouble now. but the trouble will come after the first

year. The difficulty is that the enforcement of the law may result in very serious injustice. I contend that it should not he in the power of every person to enter an action before any justice of the peace, because there would be far more serious consequences to the manufacturer than the mere fine of twenty-five cents for every ball of twine found short.
Is there any provision respecting twine that is held over and not yet sold ? There are a number of dealers that have twine that was made last year and not stamped.
The Bill will not interfere with that.
My opinion is that imported twine should be inspected while in bond, and twine manufactured here should be inspected before being shipped to the dealer. Then there would be no trouble about stamping.
Has any amendment been proposed postponing the operation of this section ?
No.
I think, then, that the question put by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Stephens) is a very pertinent one.
Every word included in this clause was in the law which came into force on the 1st of October last. The only difference is with regard to the penalty for fraudulent stamping.
Then, I do not see the point of the observations made by the hon. member for Kent. Does he refer to twine manufactured before October last?

All twine carried over by dealers was manufactured in the spring of 1900, and shipped before July of that year. A dealer ordered, let us say, twenty, forty7 or fifty tons of binder twine, getting in his stock for the season. He did not sell as much as he expected and carried over from two to ten tons. Surely he is not to be deprived of the right to sell that twine. But is it not true that if he sells it, then, under this law, the manufacturer who made it is liable to a fine for everv ball sold ?
It does not apply to twine made before the passage of the Act.
I do not see that.

There was no law to compel a man to put a tag on the twine prior to October. If, for illustration, twine was manufactured prior to last October, and was put on the market last year and was not sold but was carried over,' the fact that it was manufactured prior to last October Mr. HEYD.
' could be established, and it would not come within the law. That is clear.
It says : ' Every ball of twine offered for sale ' shall be stamped.
But read subsection 2.	[DOT]

I do not see that that affects it. The Bill applies to the present and provides that twine shall not be offered for sale unstamped, and if it is found not to be up to the standard marked on the stamp, the manufacturer or importer is liable to a penalty.

At the instance of the factories at Brantford, I wrote to the Justice Department, and they replied that the twine manufactured before the passage of the Act was not subject to the provision of the Act.

I do not think that that is the effect of this Bill. The provisions of section 6, subsection 1 are perfectly explicit. If twine is offered for sale, it must be stamped. The mere use of the words ' every manufacturer or importer ' in subsection 2 would not affect that. If the facts are as the hon. member for Kent says they are, some provision should be made. In passing, I would ask the minister what change was made in the law by this Bill. This Bill was transferred or taken from the Weights and Measures Act and incorporated into the present Act respecting the package and sale of certain staple commodities. In order to show the committee how the law stands as passed last year, I will read clause 3 of the Act, which says :
Upon or attached to every ball of binder twine offered for sale, there shall be a stamp with the name of the manufacturer or importer, stating the number of feet of twine per pound in such ball.
Subsection 2. Every manufacturer or importer who neglects to comply with the provisions of this section shall, upon summary conviction, be liable to a penalty of not less than 25 cents per ball, but no deficiency in the number of feet contained in any ball shall be deemed a contravention of this section unless such deficiency exceeds 5 per cent of the length stated upon such stamp.

This is exactly the section we have now ?
The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE Yes.

I do not understand the object of introducing the Bill unless it is to bring it under a different title. It is not necessary to re-enact the whole provision merely for the purpose of putting it under a different department.

I move that these words be added to section 0, as subsection 4 :

If that was inserted this Bill would cover all the ground that I am complaining of.

1 think the hon. gentleman is right. The last clause of the Bill as the law now stands reads as he has stated, and this clause should be added to the Bill.
It appears that I was wrong in my construction of the law in clause 3 under section 6. I would like to know to whom any one who is wronged or injured under this law shall apply for redress ?

Suppose after this is adopted an importer has on hand a large quantity of twine imported this year, and he has not got the tag upon it. What would be the law in respect to the sale of that twine ?

There is something of an anomaly in having one clause or an Act come into force at one time and the general Act at another time.

I think it is quite in order to make this amendment for the pui-pose of carrying out the purpose of the Act of last year. The corresponding section in the Act of last year provided that it should not come into force until the 1st of October. On the 1st of October it came into force and applied to binder twine offered for sale in Canada. The hon. member for Kent (Mr. Stephens) desires to preserve the provisions of this section. With the permission of the committee we will go back to section 3, which was adopted the other day, and make a change which was suggested to me. The section, as it now reads, is as follows :
3. Every barrel of salt packed in bulk, sold or offered for sale, shall contain 280 pounds of salt, and every such barrel of salt sold or offered for sale, shall have the correct gross and net weight thereof marked upon it in a permanent manner.
The only change that I propose to make will be in regard to salt in bags. The clause that I propose will read as follows :
Every barrel of salt packed in bulk, sold or offered for sale, shall contain 280 pounds of salt, and every such barrel or sack of salt sold or offered for sale shall have the correct gross weight thereof, and in the case of a barrel, the net weight also marked upon it in a plain and permanent manner.

For the information of the committee I may say that this is an amendment to the Weights and Measures Act that was passed by the House last session, and after it had passed the House it was thrown out by the Senate, on the ground, apparently, that it was unworkable. I may say that the law has been since 1888 that all barrels of salt shall have the net and gross weight stamped upon them. At that time it wa's customary for the trade to ship salt only in barrels, but in the course of time salt has been shipped in sacks as well. It is brought into the country and shipped in sacks at the present time and the manufacturers of salt are desirous that the sack shall be branded, not with the net weight, but with the gross weight of salt supposed to be contained therein. This provision last year had the full endorsatiou of the manufacturers of salt in the Dominion of Canada. It met with their approval, and was cordially endorsed by the then hon. Minister of Inland Revenue. The trade sack of salt Is supposed to contain 200 pounds. I was informed last year, and I understand the information holds good this year also, that salt has been put on the market in sacks containing considerably less than 200 pounds. The amendment is entirely in the interest of the consumers of salt. The arguments that have been made to us this afternoon, bearing on the sale of binder twine, to a large extent, hold good in reference to the sale of salt. The manufacturers of salt simply ask that it shall be required that a sack of salt shall have the gross weight stamped thereon. I do not think T need say anything further because

the subject was fully discussed in the House last session. There are some hon. members of the House who were not here last session and who may not) be familiar with it, and for their benefit, I would state that the only change in the Act, which has been on the statute-book since 1888, is the inserting of the provision that a sack of salt shall have the gross weight stamped thereon. Provision is already made in the Act for the shrinkage in salt, so that there is no need of any fear upon that score. The Act is in the interest of the honest manufacturer of salt, who desires that he shall not be placed at the mercy of a dishonest dealer who will put a sack of salt on the market ostensibly weighing 200 pounds, but which in reality weighs considerably less. Therefore, as the proposal is eminently in the interest of the consumer, I would like to see it placed upon the statute-book. I hope in doing this we shall not run counter to the Senate. The Senate threw out this provision last year, but with their increased enlightenment I hope they will be willing to endorse it this year.

I would like to concur in the remarks of the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) and to support his contention. I have sold salt ever since I can remember by the barrel and by the bag. We used to get it previously in bags from the old country. It comes from the old country in sacks weighing as much as 180 pounds, some 1G0 pounds, and some as low as 140 pounds. The standard for Canadian salt has been made by general consent probably more than anything else, 200 pounds.
Tn'o hundred and eighty pounds, is it not ?

1 am speaking of the sack which is 200 pounds. It is difficult to sell a sack containing 200 pounds of salt against one which would be imported and which would be very close to 180 pounds. There would hardly be a perceptible difference to the consumer between the two sacks, although he would get 20 pounds less in one than in the other. I can quite understand that the necessity is as great for having the weight branded upon the sacks as upon barrels. I am sure it will be well received by the trade, and it will be a protection to the consumer. I cannot say why the Senate should throw out this amendment as my hon. friend (Mr. Holmes) remarked, except, perhaps, it is that there may have been some hon. members of the Senate from the east where they are large consumers of English salt. English salt comes in free of duty and it is consumed largely in the east, in Montreal and amongst the fishermen of the maritime provinces. It does not come west of Montreal on account of the high freight. It appears to me to be inconceivable why Mr. HOLMES.
salt should not be branded in bags as well as in barrels. I heartily concur in the amendment which has been presented.

I do not wish to say very much on this subject, but, having a little knowledge of the salt business, having been a manufacturer of salt for some little time,
I may be permitted to offer a few observations. In the first place we do not intend by this amendment to make any change in the barrel of salt. It really does not touch that at all, so that barrels will remain as they are at present. They have to be stamped with the gross and net weight and the tare so that every man who buys a barrel of salt knows exactly what he is getting. Of course, the barrel is subject to 5 per cent shrinkage. I contend that that provision is not necessary. If salt is not put up too green, instead of shrinking, I think it will come out long in damp weather. Sack salt coming from the old country shrinks to a considerable extent. I think this is not right. If the salt is dry when it is put up it will not shrink any further, but ir they put up that salt within a week after it is made it will shrink very much. 1 think this amendment regarding sack salt is a very commendable one. In buying a sack of salt that is considered to contain 200 pounds, if the farmer, or fisherman, only gets 140, or 150 pounds, he does not get value for what he is paying for. The manufacturer who puts up a 200-pound sack is placed at a great disadvantage and he will be obliged to give up business if that sort of thing continues. In the United States there is a law to the effect that manufacturers must keep salt after it is made, I think, for two weeks before it is put up, and if it is put up before that time the person doing it is subject to a very heavy fine. If all the manufacturers in Canada and elsewhere were put on this basis, the salt would not shrink. Consequently you will see that the shrinking business can be avoided if they put up the salt in the proper manner. I would be glad to see this Act passed, as I believe it is in the interest of the consumers. I hope it will pass the Senate this time.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria. N.S.) It is all very w*>U to speak of salt being put up in proper packages, but when you have a large quantity shipped from Liverpool in a poor quality of bags, they are handled so hurriedly and so roughly, and trucked to the warehouse in such a manner that there is always a large shrinkage. In order to have the quantity originally shipped you will require to have different kinds of sacks altogether. I know something of this trade, because I have had occasion to buy quite largely of salt both in bulk and in bags. It is all nonsense to think that you can by Act of parliament provide that the same quantity of salt shipped from Liverpool will arrive intact here in Canada.

I might say to my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Ross) that it is not intended by this Bill to make a uniform bag of salt as in the case of a barrel of salt. A barrel of salt must contain 280 pounds in Canada, but it is not so with the bags. It is intended by this amendment to provide that the bags shall be marked with the quantity each contains, whether it be 50 pounds or 200 pounds, or any other weight. We find the most shrinkage in the English salt, but my experience has been that 5 per cent will about cover all the shrinkage, if the salt is put up properly. Under these circumstances there would be no difficulty, seeing that the manufacturer has 5 per cent shrinkage to come and go on.

As 1 come from a district where salt is largely manufactured, I wish to give my endorsa-tion to this proposed amendment. I had a conversation with the manager of the Windsor Salt Company, and he views this amendment with a great deal of approval, because while there can be no doubt that under it the consumer is protected fully, it is also a step in the direction of protecting our Canadian manufacturers as to weight.
Hear, hear.

I wish to say a few words on this question. I have handled salt for about forty years, and I think I may be considered as knowing something about this trade. It has been asserted here by some hon. gentlemen that the consumer does r.ot get value for his money, but my experience is that that is not correct. In the case of English salt, in some cases we get ten bags to the ton, and in other cases eleven bags to the ton, and the consumer is not charged for any more than he gets. The Windsor salt is put up in 50-pound, 200-pound and 280-pound barrels, and I cannot see that in any way the consumer is cheated. We weigh the bags and we know what they contain ; we always know what there is in the barrels, and therefore, the buyer does not get less than he pays for. I have been engaged in the salt business for a number of years, as I have said, and I have never known that the purchasers have been wronged.

My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Ross) says that English salt shrinks very much in weight. Well, if they dump the salt on the dock and allow the rain to get on it, that occurs through carelessness on their part, and they should be held liable for it. I do not think that my hon. friend will say that in every case they put the proper quantity of salt in the bags before they ship it to this country. The hon. gentleman cannot know that, and the object of this law is to make them do so. If the salt is put up dry and in good order it will not shrink.

It is not often that parliament is called upon by the manufacturers to legislate in the interest of the consumers, but in this case the amendments proposed are suggested by the manufacturers as a matter of protection to the consumer. There is no advantage to the manufacturers in the resolutions themselves, any more than that they protect them from what they term dishonest competition on the part of those who want to put light weight salt on the market. My hon. friend from Victoria, N.S. (Mr. Ross) says that the law will not be satisfactory to a certain portion of the community. Well, we cannot put any law on the statute-book which is not open to that objection, but I contend that this law is manifestly in the interest of the great bulk of the consumers of salt in Canada, and as such it should meet with the approval of this House.

I propose the following subsection :
To insert the words ' or sack,' after the word * barrel.'

I would like to ask the minister one question. I do not quite understand the twine clause which has been inserted. If a man offers for sale twine which was imported prior to last October, and which has no tag upon it, can he sell it without the tag ?

Yes.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hom.W. S. Fielding) delivered a Message from His Excellency the Governor General.
Mr. SPEAKER read the Message, as follows :
Minto.
The Governor General transmits to the House of Commons supplementary estimates of sums required for the service of the Dominion for the year ending 30th June, 1902, and in accordance with the provisions of the British North America Act, the Governor General recommends these estimates to the House of Commons. Government House,
Ottawa, 10th May, 1901.
Bill (No. 122) further to amend the General Inspection Act-the Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. Mr. Bernier) read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.

| The greater part of this Bill is a repetition



of the law as it now stands, but as there were complaints during last fall from foreign and British buyers with regard to the Inspection of grain coming from the United States in transit to Great Britain, and as an inquiry was held in Montreal during the winter by a commission composed of people with a knowledge of the trade, and as they recommended that changes should be made in the law, not only to satisfy the people who were making these complaints, but to protect our own trade, this Bill is introduced for the purpose of making the necessary changes. The only changes of importance are with regard to the grain inspection. The government proposes to provide for the inspection of grain east of Port Arthur, leaving the law as it is now with respect to the inspection in Manitoba. It is proposed that inspectors shall pass the examination required by the law, before a board of examiners chosen by the boards of trade of different cities, notably Montreal and Toronto. Each inspector must pass the necessary examination.
On section 2,
I would suggest to the minister the advisability of changing the word ' apples ' to the word * fruit.'
The Minister of Agriculture has a Bill before the House which provides for the inspection of fruit.
How many chief inspectors will be appointed, and where will they be stationed ?

There will be one chief inspector. I cannot say how many deputy inspectors will be appointed. In this we will be guided by the requirements of the trade.
On section 5,

I propose to alter (he Bill, and to substitute for clause C of the present law, referred to In section 5, the following
Subsections 6 and 8 of section 16 of the said Act are repealed, and the following are substituted therefor :
6. If any dispute arises between any inspector or deputy inspector and the owner or possessor of any article inspected by him, in respect of which article a chief inspector has been appointed, with regard to the quality or condition of such article, or relating thereto, the matter in dispute shall not be decided by either of the methods in this section before provided, but upon application by either of the parties to the dispute, to the secretary of the board of trade or chamber of commerce for the place where the dispute has arisen, and who have appointed a board of examiners, the secretary shall forthwith summon said board of examiners for the said place, who, or a majority of whom, shall immediately examine such article and re-Mr. BERNIER.
port in writing their opinion of the quality or condition thereof. Should the board of examiners not confirm the grading fixed by the inspector or deputy inspector, and the owner and producer, within twenty-four hours after receiving notification thereof makes further appeal, the dispute shall be referred to the chief inspector, who shall immediately examine such articles and report his opinion of the quality or condition thereof; and his determination, expressed in writing, shall be final and conclusive, and the inspector or deputy inspector shall immediately conform thereto, and shall brand, stamp or mark, or cause to be branded, stamped or marked, such article, or the package containing it, of the quality or condition ascertained by the determination aforesaid, or shall grant a certificate of inspection in accordance with such determination, as the case requires; provided that nothing herein contained shall prevent the owner appealing direct from the inspector or deputy inspector to the chief inspector, whose decision in all cases shall be final and binding on all parties; providing always that no appeal shall be considered in any case where the identity of the article in dispute has not been preserved.
I would like to ask the minister if the appointing of inspectors makes inspection compulsory ?
No. We appoint inspectors in order that those who sell for export may have a certificate to protect themselves. But, there is no compulsion.

I know something of the trade in grain, and I may explain to the hon. member for Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hackett) that it is not compulsory to inspect grain unless it is sold for export. If sold for export it must be inspected, because the railways will not take it otherwise. I would like to make sure that I understand this amendment, which I tried to follow, but which is somewhat long. If a cargo of grain is received in Montreal and should not pass inspection of the deputy, he would notify the owner of the cargo. The owner would apply to the secretary of the board of trade, who would notify a number of members of the board, and who,
I suppose, would be called a board of arbitration.
A board of examiners or board of surveys.

In every board of trade there is a board of arbitrators, and, perhaps, they would be selected from. If this board cannot decide the matter, it goes to the chief inspector, whose judgment is final. That is as I understand it.
Yes.

I think that is a fair provision. I sent a copy of the Bill to a number of grain men throughout the country who were a good deal interested, and who were apprehensive of the effect it

would have. I have had no reply from any of them, so I assume that the Bill is satisfactory. We in the trade first feared that these matters would be referred to the department at Ottawa. This, as can easily be understood, would be a great hardship. A cargo of grain might arrive at Montreal, and, if the question of grade had to be referred to Ottawa, it might be a week or ten days before it could be settled, and in the meantime, the time of contract with the intending purchaser on the other side would have expired, and the sale would be lost. But, I see now that the law would be quite workable. May I ask the minister if any provision has been made for the expense in connection with these appeals. In conversation with a Chicago merchant some time ago, I was informed that in that city, if a man made application for a board of appraisers, he paid a fee of about $5, and, if the inspection went in his favour his money was returned to him, but if it went against him, the money went to pay the expenses of the board of appraisers. How will the government deal with that matter ?
That would be settled by regulation.
I wish to express my concurrence in the Bill.

My hon. friend from Ontario (Mr. Ross) has spoken on the inspection of grain. I had in mind the inspection of fish. If the minister is going to appoint inspectors, compel inspection and *charge a fee, he is going to place a tax upon the fishermen. I would like to have a statement from the minister on that point.

It is not the intention of the government to make the inspection compulsory.
On section 6,

The only change here is in the insertion of the words ' or otherwise,' making the section read :
8. Whenever any difference arises between inspectors as to the true quality or grade of any article inspected by one of them and re-inspected by another, such difference shall be definitely determined by reference to the chief inspector, if one has been appointed, or otherwise to such board of arbitration or other authority as the Governor in Council appoints for that purpose.
Bill, as amended, reported, and read the third time and passed.
The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) moved that the House go again into Committee of Supply.

Before you leave the Chair I would like to bring the right hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that 154*
on the 1st day of this month we were informed that all the business of the House yet to be brought down would be brought down that week or early the next week. We are now in the last days of the last week referred to, and we have not yet had the measure respecting the railway subsidies. /
The railway subsidies will not be large, I hope to bring them down on Monday.
The right hon. gentleman will also permit me to mention that we have not yet the papers relating to the claim of Mackenzie & Mann. They were promised early in April.
I have not yet been able to fulfil my good intentions. They will be brought down at an early day. The railway subsidies may be expected Monday or Tuesday.
We were promised a lot of papers on the railway estimates that have not been brought down. The proposed Clergue contract has not yet been brought down.
I will take a note of it. Anything else?

I want the amount of rails laid on the Intercolonial Railway, on the Drummond Railway, all papers in reference to the coal contracts, the correspondence and tenders in reference to contracts for the purchase of locomotives, freight cars, passenger cars and other material of the Intercolonial Railway, and the correspondence and negotiations in reference to the purchase of properties at Point LGvis.
I thought my hon. friend had been put in possession, personally, of those papers.
I have only the bare contract, but no correspondence or negotiations.
May I ask the First Minister if we are correct in understanding that no other Bill is to be introduced this session regarding an increase of the judges' salaries, except what is on the paper ?
I do not think so, but I would not like to bind myself to any statement to-day.

Motion agreed to.
