House again in committee on Bill (No. 103) relating to an agreement between the
government of Manitoba and the Canadian Northern Railway Company, respecting certain railways.-Mr. Mclsaac.
Shall the preamble be adopted ?
Carried.

Mr. Chairman, I presume that the statement that this preamble shall be carried, made a moment ago by some hon. members, is only a little premature. I have no doubt it will be carried, but I have a few words to say in reference to the matter, and a few opinions to express in the direction of taking the position that the preamble of the Bill ought not to be carried whatever may be the result of this reference to this House. I was talking upon this question a night or two ago, Mr. Chairman, when you were in the Chair, and I fell a few minutes short of concluding my argument when the hour devoted to private Bills expired. I had reached the point where I proposed to attempt to demonstrate that the position of matters in Manitoba in reference to the transportation question, if no action had been taken by the legislature of that province, if no contract had been made for the purpose for which it was expected to make that contract-I was proceeding to demonstrate what, in my opinion, would have been in the near future the condition of matters in regard to the transportation problem in that province. I was about to express the opinion that the concessions in regard to freight rates which are to be secured under the provisions of the contracts in the Bill we are now considering, will, in the very near future, if the Bill passes, prove to be concessions that will be, in the rates charged, as provided by the Bill, higher than the natural course of events, the natural tendency of competition, would give the province of Manitoba. I believe, Sir, that the province of Manitoba is incurring enormous responsibilities-responsibilities that are likely to involve here in serious financial difficulties for the purpose of acquiring something that, in the natural course of events, would have come to her in two years. Hitherto Manitoba has had but one railway outlet and has not had the benefit of railway competition. Manitoba is about to have the benefit of railway competition conferred upon her, without purchase or investment of money. She has now the Canadian Pacific Railway; she will soon have a railway to Port Arthur, the line that is under consideration now, the construction of which does not depend upon the passing of this Bill. She will also have direct railway communication with the American port of Duluth at the head of Lake Superior. Within two years, probably within one year from this time, she will have three railway lines competing for the Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
transportation of her grain and merchandise to an fro from the waters of Lake Superior to the heart of the province of Manitoba. When that point is reached, when these roads are constructed, when three railway lines are competing for the business of Manitoba, I believe, Mr. Chairman, that it will be found that the rates provided for by this contract of 10 cents per hundredweight on wheat, of 15 per cent reduction in the present rates on every class of merchandise, and 3 cents per mile for passengers, with the probable exception of the passenger rate, wrill be found to be excessive and greater than the natural result of competition will confer upon the province without reference to this obligation, without reference to the great burdens which prospectively are being incurred by the province of Manitoba. The usual result of building competing lines is that at last these lines consolidate. This is not at all likely to be the case under the circumstances that I have been depicting, and I do not suppose that there is the slightest danger that the construction of these three lines in place of the one now in operation will have any other result than to give the province of Manitoba the benefit of genuine competition and a very large decrease in the rates charged for the transportation of merchandise and grain. If this is true, I ask, viewing this question from the Manitoba standpoint, what sense is there in the province incurring an obligation of $683,000 a year, the interest upon $17,075,000 at the rate of 4 per cent, for the purpose of securing something, which, the tendency of natural events, the operation of competition and the opening of new lines will inevitably give to Manitoba within the next twenty-four months ? That is the feature of the case that strikes me as being a matter which should command the attention of this House. It strikes me as being a feature of the case which renders it absolutely certain that this bargain is an improvident one, a foolish one, and that Manitoba is not acting in her own interests in embarking upon this scheme. Of course, it may be said that it As none of our business, and perhaps, in a sense, it is not. But, Manitoba is a province of this Dominion, and the interests and prosperity of Manitoba are to a greater or less extent a matter of concern to every other province and the Dominion cannot afford-if its interests will be jeopardized and affected in an injurious way-to have any one province suffering the serious consequences of any mistake they may have made which entails upon her ruinous burdens if our action can avert it. This may be entirely Manitoba's own matter and we might not be called upon to do more than extend our sympathy to Manitoba, we might not be called upon to do more than give our advice to Manitoba if we were not called upon to exercise our func-

tions as a legislature in this matter. Why is this Bill before us ? If this is purely and simply Manitoba's act, if Manitoba alone is responsible for this position of matters, what have we to do with it at all ? But, if the Bill is before us, if the Bill requires our sanction, if it requires our action to make it law, we are just as much a party to this arrangement as Manitoba is. and we cannot divest ourselves of the responsibility that rests upon us as a legislature. It is childish to say that we have nothing to do with it, that we have no responsibility when we have spent four days in the Railway Committee wrangling over this question, spent day after day in the House of Commons discussing the question, when we are discussing it to-night, and when we will be discussing it again. Why ? What business have we to discuss this question, if we have nothing to do with it ? What business have we to advance arguments pro and con, if it is a matter for which we are not responsible ? Our responsibility is just as great, is just as actual as the responsibility of the Manitoba government, and so it becomes us to look at the merits of this case, it becomes us to arrive at a conclusion as to the merits of this case, and to be governed by the evidence which is furnished to us by an investigation as to the merits of this Bill which is now before the House of Commons of Canada, asking of the House of Commons approval of its provisions, and which will not come into operation, which cannot become law. until the sovereign seal of the Dominion government is set upon the Bill. Manitoba, with the sanction of the parliament of Canada, with the connivance of the parliament of Canada, with the aid of the parliament of Canada, if the Bill becomes law, is about to incur a responsibility to the extent of $683,000 a year for something that will come in the natural course of events in certainly not more than five years from this date. It is a bargain characterized by a degree of improvident folly that never has characterized any proposition placed before any legislative body on the American continent since the American revolution.
When you come to examine the provisions of this Bill it is deftly and, adroitly drawn. I may justly compliment the speculators, the railroad men, the contractors with the province of Manitoba for the shrewdness and grasp that they have shown in preparing the provisions of this Bill.
They have lots of practice.

They have lots of practice ; and we have a class of public men in America, fewer thank God in Canada than in the United States, who have lots of practice in that kind of business and who can sweep the wealth of the people into
their coffers, already overflowing, with a degree of skill which is perfectly astounding. The Bill provides that periods of two years shall be arranged for arriving at a conclusion as to whether the receipts of the road after paying running expenses will pay the rental and charges that the, Manitoba government is responsible for. If there should be a deficiency in one year and a surplus in the other the two years are blocked together. But, if there should be two years deficiency and these should be followed by two years of a large surplus, not one cent of the surplus of the second period of two years can be applied to the deficiency the Manitoba government will be called on to pay for the first period of two years. The thing is blocked out in that shape so that Manitoba can pay when there is a deficiency, and the road can profit where there is a surplus. The arrangement is : heads I win, tails you lose. It is a very nice arrangement for McKenzie & Mann, but not so nice an arrangement for the province of Manitoba. Then we have an arrangement in this Bill about working expenses. It is a nice arrangement for the railroad men ; it is skilfully drawn ; it is contained in clause 11 of schedule B. It is as follows :
For the purposes of this clause the term * working expenditure ' shall not include-
See how disinterested they are at the start.
For the purposes of this clause the term ' working expenditure ' shall not include the salary or remuneration of any officer, employee or other person whose time is not wholly employed bona fide in connection with the said lines of railway in this clause mentioned ; but as to officers and employees and other persons whose services are necessary or desirable in connection with the said lines and whose whole time is not taken up in connection therewith there shall be included reasonable remuneration for the time actually expended and services actually rendered by them in connection with said lines ;
If my lion friends behind me here do not stop talking they will miss the wording of this clause, which is very important.
-and the said term shall not include any expenses, payments or outgoings not reasonably necessary for the efficient management, maintenance, operation and repair of the said lines, nor shall the said term include the cost of double tracking the said lines, but siding reasonably required for the traffic and operation of the lines shall not be deemed double tracking.
Well, when you get at this from a railway man's standpoint, what does it mean ? It means that no mortal thing in connection with construction account, or the operation of that railway shall be excluded from the term ' operating expenses,' except the laying down of the double track It covers as operating expenses, the re-railing of the line. Our friends are laying down a rather light rail now. They want the $30,400 per mile applied to the road that cost $15,000 a mile.

to go as far as possible, and so they are laying down a light rail. And when the time comes to remove that 56-pound rail or whatever it is, and put down a 90-pound rail, the substitution of the heavy for the light rail will be a part of operating expenses. The operating expenses will cover sidings ; it will cover ballasting and it wdll cover renewing bridges. The Canadian Pacific Railway came here a few years ago to get its bridge material free of duty when the time came to renew bridges, and the Canadian Northern will have charged to ' operating expenses' this charge for renewing bridges when the time comes, and the province of Manitoba will have to pay it. It will cover everything except double tracking. It will cover the construction of elevators ; the construction of warehouses ; the construction of station houses ; the construction of spur lines and branch lines. It will cover enough to swamp and absorb all the earnings of that road in * operating expenses,' and leave the province of Manitoba to pay the guarantees. That will be the inevitable result for a time at least.
Then we have no provision made in this contract with regard to freight upon materials. There is a railroad extending from Port Arthur to Winnipeg and extending beyond Winnipeg ; having already reached the western boundaries of Manitoba and beyond it. It is intended to carry this line to the Yellow Head Pass and ultimately from the Yellow Head Pass to the Pacific ocean. Over that railway from Port Arthur west, a vast amount of construction material is to be carried : rails, fish-plates, spikes, bridge material, building material, tens of thouands of tons of road material; and there is no provision made, no safeguard to protect the rights of Manitoba in this regard. And this vast amount of freight may be carried by the Canadian Northern Railway practically at the cost and expense of the province of Manitoba by putting on freight rates so nominal and ridiculously low that they amount to nothing. Everything in connection with this contract is in favour of the railway corporation, and nothing whatever, nothing that can be dreamed or imagined is in favour of the province of Manitoba. We have then this agreement fairly launched : the province of Manitoba liable for $683,000 a year; we have a schedule of freight rates arranged that will in less than two years be lower than the mark now arranged by natural competition. We have the province making itself liable for $17,000,000 for nothing, and we have the province entering into this obligation under the mistaken assumption that they have control over the rates when they possess no such control, and when the changes in this amended Bill set forth definitely that the legislature of Manitoba was labouring under a mistaken impression in that. We have clearly stated here in the amended Bill that the talk about I Mr. CHARLTON.
the control of the rates was a misnomer and a delusion, and that the Dominion government has the paramount authority and the Manitoba government subordinate authority in connection with this matter. It is true that the Dominion government, as is claimed by Manitoba, may fix maximum i-ates, and Manitoba by its arrangement with the contractors may secure lower than the maximum rates, but it is also true that the Dominion government may for reasons of public policy increase the rates. It is true that the Dominion government is master of the situation.
If the schedule of rates secured by Manitoba interfered with the rates on the Ontario business, on the 290 miles of road between the boundary of Manitoba and Port Arthur, circumstances might arise to call on the Governor in Council to upset the whole arrangement and raise these rates to a certain extent for the protection of the interests of the province of Ontario. Or, if the arrangement of rates on these roads had the practical effect of drawing business from Canadian lines to American lines, and thereby drawing to the harbour of Duluth business that we might wish to have centred at Port Arthur or Fort William, the Railway Committee of the Privy Council could step in and change these rates at their pleasure. Manitoba is absolutely powerless in the hands of the Dominion government, and has incurred vast responsibilities and vast liabilities for what was presumed to be something tangible, but what is intangible and worthless, in view of the developments in competition that will result from other railway lines being constructed in the near future, and the outcome will probably be, under the manipulation of these shrewd railway contractors, that the province of Manitoba will pay all or nearly all the guarantees provided for by the terms of this contract.
This is not a very pleasant prospect to face for the province of Manitoba, and it is not a very pleasant position for the House of Commons to force a province into ; and if that disaster can be averted honourably, if Manitoba can be saved from the consequences of her own folly ; if we, in the exercise of our sovereign power as the highest legislative body in this Dominion, having. referred to us a Bill which requires our sanction and our action-If we can avert this calamity, it is our duty to do so. It is not asked that this Bill be disallowed ; it is not asked that it be refused. It is simply asked, in the light of the facts brought out by the discussion, that Manitoba be granted an opportunity of again passing upon this matter, and of saying whether this Bill, which has been materially altered in this House, is still one which meets with her approval ; and if. when that Bill is referred back, the legislature of Manitoba, with all the facts in their possession, sanction it and declare that it meets their wishes, enough

said. We have performed our duty ; we have given Manitoba an opportunity to retrace her steps in an act of folly ; and if she will persist in that act, then the argument will come in that Manitoba must judge for herself and must suffer the consequences of her own act.
As I have said, the rates provided by this contract will, by the natural tendency of business operations, very soon prove to be excessive rates. A rate of 10 cents per 100 pounds upon wheat, for a distance of less than 500 miles, from Wininpeg to Port Arthur, is a large rate. Wheat is carried from Chicago to New York, a distance of
1.000	miles, for from 8 to 12 cents per 100 pounds. Wheat can be carried from Buffalo to New York, a distance of 450 miles, for 24 cents per 100 pounds, and yield a fail-margin ; and it is carried from Buffalo to New York by rail for 3 cents a bushel. Wheat is carried from Chicago to Montreal -transhipped at Depot Harbour, passed over the Canada Atlantic line, and laid down in Montreal-for 3$ cents a bushel, or about 5 cents per 100 pounds-a rail route almost as long as from Winnipeg to Port Arthur, besides the water transportation from Chicago to Depot Harbour. In the light of these facts, the rates provided by this contract will prove to be excessive ; and when these three lines of road are constructed, the question would settle itself, and Manitoba would secure rates as low as those provided for without having incurred one cent of obligation. And when these facts are made known, when Manitoba is placed in full possession of the knowledge that affects her interests in this matter, why should we refuse to that province an opportunity to retrace her steps, to avoid an act of folly, and to say whether she is still of opinion that she had better ratify and confirm that Bill.
There is another consideration in connection with this matter. I recollect when it cost 25 cents a bushel to transport wheat from Chicago to Buffalo, and I know that within recent years it has been done for from 1} to 2 cents a bushel. At that time it cost 45 cents a bushel to send wheat from Chicago to New York by rail. Within the last fifteen years freight rates upon railroads and freight rates by vessels have been reduced to the extent of two-thirds. The rate now is one-third the rate paid not more than ten or fifteen years ago ; and the tendencies which constantly work for the reduction of these rates are still in operation. With improvements in railway carriage, the ultimate result has not yet been reached. We. have the 90-pound rail, the fish-plate joint, the locomotive capable of drawing forty cars of fifty tons each-
2.000	tons of freight-with a crew of four or five men ; and still there are greater possibilities in the future. We may have the 120-pound rail : we may have grades still further reduced ; we may have a 100-ton car ; we may have the 4,000-ton load for
a train, and a reduction of freight rates to one-half what they are now ; and in ten years this lease, which is costing the province of Manitoba a pledge of $083,000, may be absolutely worthless. What is to be the development with regard to electric roads, which are just in their infancy, and with regard to other improvements ? We do not know what the conditions of this transportation problem will be in a single decade ; and the province of Manitoba is incurring a vast risk in assuming any responsibility whatever in this matter. She had better sit down and let the stars run their course-let events take their counse, and let the progress that the world is now making redound to her advantage in a few years, and secure to her rates far below the scale for which she is paying $17,000,000 to-day. And why should Manitoba, at great cost and risk, pay for an imagined right to fix rates, which the Dominion may revise at pleasure, and Which may, as I have pointed out, soon be entirely excessive ? Why should Manitoba pay for this privilege ? Why should Manitoba buy the barren right to fix rates which this government may supersede and override ? Why should she pay to get herself into a position where she will be -worse off in five years, inevitably, than she will be if she sits still and does nothing?
There are other things about this contract. Why do not these gentlemen give to Manitoba representation upon the railway board ? She incurs all the liability for the payment of the bonds and the rental of $7,000,000 worth of roads bought from the Northern Pacific ; she sets up Mackenzie & Maun in business, and assumes all the responsibilities they incur ; and they do not even give her the miserable privilege of having a single representative on the board -not an individual to watch her interests, to watch the possible manipulation of speculators, who. perhaps, will override her interests, and whose operations, it may be very desirable to have some competent man to watch and check. No, she has no representation upon the board, nor can she appoint an auditor. Why is not Manitoba permitted to name an auditor to audit the accounts when she is ultimately liable for the last cent ? She has neither representation on the board, nor the privilege of appointing an auditor, nor any other privilege, except the privilege of paying the cost, and she will have that privilege to her heart's content.
These gentlemen who are interested in this contract, about how badly have they been treated anyway by the Dominion government and the Ontario and other governments ? They are building a road, and are receiving aid from the Dominion and Ontario governments to the amount of $10,400 per mile, and they have agreed, as a condition of receiving that aid. that the Dominion shall exercise the right, with regard to rates, that they are now selling to Manitoba for $17,000,000. Is not that rather

sharp practice ? And Manitoba has guaranteed their bonds to the extent of .$20,000 a mile, and they are placed In possession of resources amounting to $30,400 per mile on a road that will only cost half the money. They are placed in possession of resources by the act of the Dominion government and the act of the Ontario government and the endorsation of the Manitoba government, that will build two miles for every mile they have to build; and having built their road to Rainy River, they will have the means to go on and build 300 miles more out of these resources. And yet this is not enough. And so they proceed to get this contract, and get Manitoba to agree to become sponsor for these vast operations-the purchase of the whole system of the Northern Pacific in Manitoba, the guaranteeing of the bonds of the road from Port Arthur to Rainy River, and the guaranteeing of other sections, amounting in all to the round sum of $700,000 per year. Well, I think that when these gentlemen got bonuses almost sufficient to build their line, and in addition got a guarantee of $20,000 a mile, and were placed in a position to build two miles of road for every mile covered by their guarantee and bonds, they were well enough off, and there was no necessity for them to ask further concessions and proceed to gobble up the wdiole province.
I believe that it is asserted that no representations were made, when this measure was under discussion in the Manitoba legislature, that would lead the members of that legislature to suppose that Manitoba would exercise control over railway rates. I have here a few extracts from speeches and from editorials in Manitoba papers with regard to this question, and I find that Premier Roblin, speaking in the Manitoba legislature upon the consideration received by the province as a quid pro quo for its pledged credit, made use of this language. Referring to the pledge of the credit of the province, and the assumption of these liabilities, he said :
That means that the people of Manitoba will enjoy a privilege enjoyed by no other province in Canada or state in the United States, that the Lieutenant Governor in Council will have the right and authority to make all tariffs from that time forward until the contract Is revoked.
What would be the inference drawn from that language ? It would be that the province of Manitoba was incurring obligations in return for which she should control rates, and I believe that the majority of the members of the Manitoba legislature took the same view of the case. Further on the premier said :
The country might, he felt, look forward with
confidence to the future

I think it may, but a different kind of future from that he is referring to.

-as this railway policy would be the inauguration of a new era of prosperity and growth, particularly in an agricultural sense, that would be a wonder and marvel to other parts of Canada, because of the confidence that would be established by the fact that the government, the people, controlled the rates, and would be an encouragement to the farmers to increase the area of land they cultivated, and their herds, and show the enterprise and development that a flourishing condition of things would warrant.
By getting a rate of 10 cents a hundred weight on wheat, when, in two years, natural competition would probably bring it down to 7 or 8 cents. By getting 15 per cent off the present schedule rates on the Canadian Pacific Railway, when the natural trend of events and competition will bring them down 40 per cent at least. These magnificent results are heralded to the people of Manitoba and the Dominion as the outcome of a great stroke of statesmanship that would make Manitoba the envy of all the provinces of this Dominion, and all the states of the American republic. Bosh ! What nonsense !
And we should take into consideration that statements of this kind did have their influence, did undoubtedly tend tq produce, if they did not absolutely procure, the action taken by the Manitoba government; and if I am capable of drawing a conclusion, it is that it is our duty, in the face of all these representations made, not to reverse the action of Manitoba, not to set our veto on any right which that province possesses, but to exercise the right we possess now-when called upon, in a cooperative and co-ordinate capacity to sanction this legislation-only to sanction it subject to the condition that it shall be referred back to the province of Alanitoba, with the changes we have made, and the considerations that have been developed, for their action and approval again.
I have also here an extract from a speech made by the Attorney General of Manitoba, Air. Campbell. I do not know but that it would be merely an act of fairness to read that extract, so that the charge could not be made that there was any attempt to prejudice or pettifog this case. Mr. Campbell, in a speech upon this question, while it was under consideration, made use of the following language :
Now we come to the most important part of the contract, in connection with which a great deal of discussion has arisen, namely, the imposition of tolls. There are gentlemen who desire to mystify the public in reference to this question. It is stated tjiat the government cannot do what a private individual might do.
The Minister of Railways has laid down this proposition clearly and distinctly, that all the Dominion government does is to fix the maximum tariff. The Railway Act and the charter of the company give it the power to make and impose the tariff, that is to say, it must go to the Dominion government for sanction; and we know the practice that prevails in the sanction of it. The government simply say what

toll shall be the maximum toll. Now, the Railway Committee are permitted, and I have no doubt that hon. gentlemen who have anything to do with traffic know what they are allowed to contract within that maximum tariff. We find that this is done upon passenger rates; the rate is 3 cents a mile according to the maximum tariff, yet we find railways running cheap tares, cheap excursions, and if they were not permitted to contract at a less sum than the maximum tariff it would not be possible to get the benefit of these cheap fares. At the same time, we find there is a tariff for carrying freight at a certain figure, yet the company are permitted, as Mr. Blair pointed out, to make whatever contract they like within that limit. Now, all the government is attempting to do is what each individual is doing for himself-that we are endeavouring to do for the whole people. That is to say, while I myself might go and make a contract, the government proposes to make that contract for the whole of the people of the province. The sections that deal with this matter state that there should be no discrimination, no special rates, and no secret special rates, and there are other restrictions. Now. if the contract we propose to make were a discriminatory contract, it might be had under the Railway Act; but we are making a contract which is just and equitable, and applies equally to every person in Manitoba. It is quite true that if we make a contract at a greater rate than that fixed as a maximum tariff by the Dominion, our contract would be superseded by the general tariff fixed by the government at Ottawa; but that would be no detriment to the people of this province, because we would get the benefit of the lowest tariff, whichever it might be. If the Dominion government made a lower tariff than the amount we had fixed, the people of the province would get the benefit of it; but if our contract for rates was lower than the maximum, the people would get the benefit of that, and that is what we propose to do. We have no objection to the Minister of Railways or the government at Ottawa, if they think fit, to make a lower tariff than we suggest; the people will have no quarrel with them, because we will receive the benefit of whichever is the lowest tariff.
A great deal has been said about the Dominion government not allowing us to encroach upon their rights under the Railway Act. We do not desire to encroach upon the rights of the Dominion government, and I believe when the Dominion government come to ratify this contract, as they will be shortly called upon to do, they will say, as it is proper for them to say, that they reserve to themselves to fix any amount that they like, and if the amount is less than the amount we fixed no harm is done.
That is the statement of Mr. Campbell, and it will he observed that he states plainly that the Dominion government may fix maximum rates. But he does not state that the Dominion government may increase the rates, that it may override the action of Manitoba in any direction or in any manner that it may deem advisable in the public interest; and he does not state that the putting of rates below a reasonable figure, while it would benefit the people of Manitoba so far as freight rates are concerned, would leave the people of Manitoba to pay the deficiency which was caused by putting rates below a proper figure. And he does not say to the
people of Manitoba that these rates that he is talking about, which the Dominion government may revise, which the Dominion government may increase, and which, If lower than a paying rate the government of Manitoba must make up indirectly if not direct^-he does not say that these rates are, in any event probably higher than the actual natural rates charged for business will be within two or three years, when other railway lines are completed, and when Manitoba is enjoying the benefits of competition that will come without guarantee, without liability, without incurring the obligations he would recommend.
So, Mr. Chairman, I do not think that even the language of Attorney General Campbell will set aside the assertion I make, that the impression in the legislature of Manitoba and among the people of Manitoba was that though the province was incurring this obligation of $683,000 a year for one year less than one thousand years, a period far longer than the average of empires and nations, yet in return for that obligation she was getting absolute control of rates, when the truth is that she has not such control, the Dominion having paramount authority, the Railway Committee of the Privy Council can treat these rates in any manner it chooses-if the public interests require it the rates can be raised as well as lowered, the interests of Ontario against discriminating rates can be protected by raising them, the business can be diverted from foreign roads by raising the rates, and therefore, Manitoba has been buying an apparent privilege, n shadow without substance, but she has been incurring an obligation which is not a shadow, except as it renders dark and gloomy her future for years to come.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Amen.

' Amen,' says the hon. member (Mr. LaRiviere), and a great many in Manitoba in the future, when the pinch comes and the taxes are being collected and when the effects of this act of supreme folly make themselves felt, will pray for the vengeance of heaven on the men that brought in the Bill, and will fervently say ' Amen.'
This Bill that we are considering here tonight is not the Bill that the legislature of Manitoba considered ; it is a part of it. But we have amended the Bill ; we have made essential amendments. We have incorporated a clause here-it was necessary in the interests of honesty and fair-play, necessary to apprise the people of Manitoba of the actual position of the matter; necessary for the purpose of showing that they had not and could not have absolute control of rates. But X hold that, as we have inserted that provision, the Bill is so essentially amended and the purport of it so en-. tirely different from what the Manitoba

legislators and the Manitoba public suppose, that it is merely an act of the most common kind of fair-play to refer that Bill back to these people with these changed conditions and ask them what they think of them. If it is suitable and agreeable, let them ratify it, and if not, give them a chance to get out of the mess they have, got into. Now, what are these changes ? Section 3 says :
3. Nothing in this Act or in the indentures contained in the schedules hereto, or done in pursuance of this Act or or the said indentures, shall-
(a)	divest or limit, temporarily or otherwise, the rights or powers (under existing or future legislation of the parliament df Canada) of the Governor in Council, or of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, or of any commission or other authority, respecting any matter or thing, obligation or duty;
(b)	place the government of Canada, directly or indirectly, under any liability, obligation or duty with respect to any payment, matter or thing in the said indentures provided for or referred to ;
(c)	authorize the Canadian Northern Railway Company to charge or demand any higher rates for the carriage of freight or passengers than those heretofore or hereafter fixed, under the authority of existing or future legislation of the parliament of Canada, by the Governor in Council, or by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, or by any commission or other authority.
Absolutely sweeping away every vestige of primary authority that the legislature of Manitoba supposed that that province might, under the contract, possess, absolutely changing the condition of the contract as understood by the people of Manitoba, clearly defining, absolutely asserting that the Dominion government was paramount in authority, and the Manitoba government subordinate in authority, with reference to this matter. Now, this is a disillusion to the people of Manitoba. If this position had been clearly stated, I do not believe that the people of Manitoba would ever have ratified this contract; and I am desirous of putting to the test whether the opinion that I entertain with regard to that matter is correct, by actually giving to the people of Manitoba an opportunity to pass upon the amended provisions of this contract.
What about the resolution on short speeches ?

With regard to short speeches, I have exhausted my efforts in that direction, and I have concluded to convert the House by adopting opposite tactics, and if I can, by making three or four long speeches, induce my hon. friend the leader of the government and others to consider the propriety of referring this question to a special committee for the purpose of seeing if the abuse can be averted, I shall think my efforts have been successful.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Don't forget to read the Scriptures.

The Scriptures are so distasteful to my hon. friend that I won't venture to read them again. Now, it might be a very pertinent question to ask at this juncture : What are our functions here, anyway ? What are we talking about ? Why are we talking about this thing ? Is this all wind ? Is this without purpose ? Have we not a right to talk about this question ? Can we produce any effect by talking about this question ?
Not the least.

No, I guess not. Has parliament jiower to do anything with this question ? It is quite evident what it will do. It reminds me of a story told some years ago when the Pennsylvania legislature was under the dominion of the Pennsylvania Railway. The manager of the road was old Jim Scott, and one of the members of the legislature, when the business of the session was about to close, said, rising to his feet : Mr. Speaker, I move that if Jim Scott had nothing else for us to do, we adjourn. Evidently Jim Scott has something for this House to do. I do not suppose that I am producing any impression here. I do not suppose that if I argued this case till doomsday I would produce any impression. But I do suppose that this House has jurisdiction, I do suppose that this House has certain functions in connection with this matter, I do suppose that this House has power to do justice or to refuse justice, that this House has power to save Manitoba or to ruin Manitoba. If we are acting in our sovereign capacity as the Dominion House of Commons, and are acting upon a Bill that we can either give or refuse our assent to, and it is strictly within our rights to do one thing or the other, I say it is not an impertinent question. What are our functions ? Our functions are positive functions, they are proper functions, they are the functions of a legislative body dealing with an Act of legislation referred to them for their action. We must stand or fall upon the verdict we give with regard to this matter.

Before this item passes, I would like to ask the hon. Minister of the Interior who his agents in Ireland are ?
Mr. Webster and Mr. Kelly.
Where is Mr. Devlin ?
In Dublin.

Is that in Ireland ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
It was when I was there.

What salary does Mr. Devlin get ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Three thousand dollars a year.

What does he do for it ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
I understand he works very hard all the time.

I notice by some of the papers that Mr. Devlin is writing letters slandering members of the House of Commons in a very blackguardly fashion. I draw the attention of the hon. minister to the fact.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.My attention was	called to	the fact to
which the hon. gentleman refers to-day. I say at once that I very much regret that these letters have been written, and I shall express my opinion of it to Mr. Devlin without delay. I take the ground at once that it is entirely improper for officers of the civil service to write letters in the newspapers reflecting upon members of the House of Commons.

I may say further that while he is criticising in the most scurrilous manner in which he has done, members of parliament, so far as I am concerned, his statements are untrue, because I think I absolutely refrained from criticising the individuals employed in Ireland.
I know that is correct.

This person has taken advantage of his position to write a letter attacking those who gave him no ground for doing so, but I am glad the hon. minister takes the ground so promptly that no civil servant has any right to attack a member of parliament in the performance of what he conceives to be his duty in the
House of Commons. I am glad to say that so far as I can see, while civil servants hold their opinions in political matters, and are quite right in so doing, neither Grit nor Tory interferes in any way in political matters. I think we may further congratulate ourselves upon the fact that the civil servants that were appointed by the government of Mr. Mackenzie, by the late government, and by the present government realize and appreciate the position of civil servants which should be that of noninterference in political matters, and more especially non-interference with members of parliament in the performance of their public duties.
To provide for expenses of an exhibit of the products of the North-west at the Pan-American exhibition at Buffalo, $4,000.
Is this going to be a separate exhibition, or in a building belonging to Canada, or is it all to be in one building ?
This is to be an exhibition made in the same manner as ordinary exhibitors go in. They go in under the regulations of the grant.

You are not going to try the foolish experiment that you tried at Chicago of erecting a separate building?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
No, there is no intention of doing that.

Are you appointing a commissioner to represent the North-west Territories, and if so, whom ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
We have not appointed anybody specially at all.

Do you intend appointing anybody ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
No. there is no present intention of appointing anybody. The Dominion commissioner is there, and there has been no arrangement made to appoint a special commissioner for the North-west. This matter is being arranged by the North-west government. It is quite impossible for the department to arrange the details of the exhibition. It may be necessary to send somebody down with the exhibits, but we will appoint no special commissioner.
Government of the Yukon Territory-Further amount required for expenses connected with the administration of the Yukon territory, $45,000.
What is this further amount required for ?

I think I explained this item when my main estimates were under consideration. I explained to the committee at the time that we had found it necessary to make

new arrangements last fall in respect to the living allowances of the officers in the Yukon, and instead of providing them with houses, as has been done by the Public Works Department, we made them a special allowance of $50 a month for lodging. The expenses of the Public Works Department are reduced in the neighbourhood of that amount-perhaps not exactly that amount-and the expenses of this department are increased by that amount. The result of having allowed them $50 a month for living allowance is that we have a large additional amount of pay in this year. This is made up in this way: Up to the first of October last, the officials were residing in a building provided for them by the Public Works Department, and the government allowed them $100 a month for living allowance. That was not satisfactory, so it was decided to let them make their own arrangements in regard to lodgings, to relieve the Public Works Department from that duty and to allow them $50 a month additional in each case for lodgings. There are between sixty and seventy officials coming under this arrangement, so that we will require $27,000. In connection with the visit of the Governor General to Dawson, the expenses being incurred by the Yukon council, when the Governor General went to Dawson, I gave instructions that he should be properly looked after by the authorities, and as there was an expense of $4,000 incurred, I am asking for that amount. We are short also on the expenditure in connection with printing, stationery and advertising. The amount exceeded the amount which we thought it would reach last year, owing to the very large number of sales of mining claims which have been made, and which have to be extensively advertised. The expenses in connection with advertising in the newspapers have been heavier than we anticipated they would be. We are asking for $4,000 on account of that. In connection with the sales of these claims, and the collection of the royalty, we have to pay commissions to the officers of the mounted police. We have concluded that is the most satisfactory way to collect the royalty. For the commission paid to the officers and fees to the auctioneers, we estimate $10,000 for this year. These amounts were not covered in the vote taken last year.

Do you pay commission to the mounted police, in addition to their usual salary ?
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR, l'es.
1 thought it was getting cheaper to live in the Yukon rather than dearer, because of the increased transportation facilities.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: In some wrays it is cheaper now than before, but our reports are that our officers have very serious difficulty in making ends meet there. I think that the House will agree that it is not desirable that the officials of the government in the Yukon should be so placed as not to be able to live in a respectable way. The general feeling appears to have been always that we have rather erred on the side of not paying our Yukon officials enough. We think this arrangement is satisfactory without being unduly extravagant.
Do you give them $50 a month for rent, and $100 for living allowance, besides their salary ?
Yes.
That seems to be pretty generous.
It looks large to us here, but if my hou. friend saw what every little thing costs in the Yukon, he would agree that this is not an extravagant arrangement.

As the Minister of the Interior has largely the control of the expenditures and the business of the Yukon, 1 would like to know what is the total Yukon expenditure proposed for the current year for all the departments ?
I will give the hon. gentleman a statement when the House meets on Monday.
I would also like to know the estimated population of the Yukon.
My deputy says that we can give a fair estimate of that.

I would like to ask the minister if one Mr. H. H. Norwood is at present employed in the Yukon ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
No.
Was he employed ?
Yes.

When did his services cease ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
About a year ago.

Has he not been employed by the	department	within jt year 1The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
It is about a year ago.
Was he employed by the department subsequent to June, 1900 ?
I think I am quite safe in saying he was not.

There are some items in the Auditor General's Report in connection with the expenditures of this gentleman, but they seem to end on June 30, 1900. He has not been in the employ of the government since June ?
It is impossible to remember to a day or two, but I am quite safe in saying that he was not.
He was not in the employ of the department in October and November last year ?
Of 1900, no.
I would like the minister to tell me, though it is not in his department, what is the salary of the postmaster at Dawson City ?
My deputy tells me that it is $3,000 a year. I do not remember, but I think it must be in the report of the Postmaster General.
My information is that he gets $1,800 a year living allowance in addition to that.
I presume so. It is outside of my department, and I cannot speak positively.
When these items are going through it is a pity the ministers are not here to give information.
If the hon. gentleman only wants to get the information at his disposal, 1 can give it to him on Monday with the other information.

I would be obliged if you would. The ministers used to say, we will give you the information on concurrence, and last year they simply called out the number of the item, and jumped from one page to another, so that we could not know what item was passing. Whatever information we get this year we will have to get it before concurrence, and then let concurrence go through as rapidly as the ministers desire.
Dominion Lands-Chargeable to income, $11,600.
How many extra clerks have you at the head office who are paid out of this vote ?

The latter portion of this vote is for the purpose of paying the copying clerks who are employed writing the patents. We did not take quite enough in the main estimates,
and we ask $1,000 more. My deputy tells me that there are four at the present time.
Are they employed solely on the patents ?
There are four originally. There are about twelve specially employed in copying patents.

Will the minister tell us what the dates of these patents are, and what progress is being made in issuing patents to the Canadian Pacific Railway under their contract with the government ?
I would like him to give us a somewhat definite statement with regard to that.

I went into the matter somewhat carefully a couple of weeks ago. and the result justifies the statement that we shall be able, without any question, to issue patents for all the lands that have been agreed upon with the Manitoba and North-west railway companies, including the Canadian Pacific Railway, by the end of this calendar year. At the present time we have issued patents for all the Canadian Pacific Railway lands that have been selected in the province of Manitoba and a large number in the Territories.

The patents are dated as of this year ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
The patent is dated when it is issued, of course.

And therefore the company will be able to claim, and I have no doubt they do claim, that their exemption on all that land dates from this year, instead of dating, as it should, from the time those lands were granted, seventeen years ago.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Let me say to my hon. friend on that point that the date of the patent makes no difference whatever. It operates from the day the land is delivered.

Will the minister tell us what progress has been made in regard to submitting to the courts the question as to when the exempton dates from ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.I am	speaking subject	to correction; but
from what I remember as I looked into the question, it would be necessary for the twenty years' period to run. An assessment of the land should be made in order that the matter could be brought into the courts. I do not know whether an assessment can be made this year or not. If it can be, we will have that done.

Then you intend to raise the question in connection with some

land that will be assessed in the North-west. You do not intend to make a straight reference to the courts in the form of a question ?

I have had some conversation with my hon. friend the Solicitor General on that subject. Though a member of the legal profession, I am of course not the legal adviser of the government. I understand that the Solicitor General takes the view that a straight reference to the court in the form of a question would not be satisfactory. I am inclined to agree with his view. ' I am speaking without desiring to be bound by wliat I am saying as to the result; when I say that I think the government will arrive at the conclusion that in order to get the question before the courts it will be necessary to have an actual assessment made and taxation based on that assessment, and the question raised as to the validity of the taxation.

Then it is the intention of the government to support the view that the assessment began twenty years from the time the land was grantable, the same as the time the subsidy was payable? What is the contention you intend to maintain when you submit the question to the courts, as to when the exemption ceases ?
That is, as to whether it was twenty years from the time the land was actually'earned by the construction of the road ?

The government must have a policy on this matter, and the minister has assured the country that he intends to uphold the settlers' view, that the exemption ceased twenty years after the land was grantable, and my contention is that it was grantable at the very time the money was payable and was paid. When this case goes to court, does the minister intend to maintain the settlers' view, or what is the view he intends to maintain, or has he formed an opinion with regard to it ?

That is a matter we shall have to submit to the legal advisers of the Crown, upon the possibility of success. This question was asked in the House some time ago, and I then stated that we would take the advice of the law officers of the Crown as to what view most favourable to the people we could establish. The most favourable view would be that the twenty years ran from the date of the contract. I question very much if the law officers of the Crown will advise us to proceed on that basis. My impression is that it is extremely likely that they would advise us that we would not be particularly likely to succeed in that contention, but that we would be more likely to succeed in the contention that the exemp-
tion should date from the time the lands were earned. On these matters we shall be guided by consultation with the law officers of the Crown.
Where would a record be found of the lands patented from time to time ? Would it be in the report of the minister ?

The record of all the Dominion lands patented is kept in the Department of the Interior. In the North-west Territories and in the province of Manitoba, where there is a land titles office under the Torrens system, the patents are forwarded to the registrar and recorded there also.

What report is there that would be available for examination by members of this House ? Would the record be kept in such a way that we could distinguish railway lands from ordinary lands taken up as homesteads ?

It has not been customary to make a detailed statement in the report of the Department of the Interior of the lands actually patented. If it is desired by the House, a special blue-book could be issued containing them. It would involve a great deal of work.
Why should it involve a very large amount of work ? You have the records in the department, and it would only mean a little copying.

What I understand my hon. friend to suggest is that there should be a blue-book issued which would show the lands patented by the Crown, distinguishing the lands patented to railway companies and to private individuals.
No, it was merely to ascertain what quantity was patented, and to what railway companies.

There would be no difficulty in putting in the annual report a statement simply giving the total quantities. The department at present shows the number of letters patent issued, and I think also the number of acres. I will make a note of the hon. gentleman's request and have the information put in the report, showing the quantity of land patented and the number of patents issued to the Canadian Pacific Railway and private individuals.
Has the Torrens land system proved a success in the North-west ?

It is found very satisfactory. Indeed, it is the finest system of land transfer in the world. In Manitoba, after some years of experience, we found it possible to make some changes in matters of detail, which have

made the system as nearly perfect as any system of land transfer can be.

the outside service	 $ 6,600
