Further amount required to complete surveys for the year, $30,000.

We sent out four parties last year, and the expenditure was estimated at $5,000 each for three of the parties, and $8,000 for Mr. Tyrrell's party. It is found, however, that the expenditure considerably exceeded the estimate, and we have to make up the deficiency.
What are these surveyors doing ?

Subdividing land for settlement. I may say that practically our work is confined to an attempt to keep ahead of settlement. We receive demands from different points saying that settlers are going in and we must send parties there to subdivide. It is impossible for us to have a general system covering the whole country, for we should spend on enormous amount of money and could not get the work done which requires to be done.
How are these men paid- by the day ?

When these surveyors are employed by the day, the chief of the party, who must be a Dominion lands surveyor, qualified under the Dominion Lands Act, gets $5 a day. The assistant, who is not required to be a Dominion lands surveyor, but who must have professional qualifications, gets $3 a day. But a large portion of the work is done under contract. The rates are fixed by the surveyor general. They are not uniform.
What are the rates ?
The surveyors under contract are paid so much a square mile. I cannot give the exact figures, but it usually runs about 7 cents per acre.
And the surveyors get their keep in addition ?
When they do the work under contract, they supply themselves ; when we pay them by the day we pay expenses.

Has the attention of the minister been called to a proposition that new territory should be laid out in townships of circular form and the farms should be segments of circles, rather than the rectangular form now followed ?

I do not think that anything of that kind has ever been brought officially before me. But I remember that a proposition was made and discussed not that the land should be laid out in circular form, that it should be laid out in such a way that roads running diagonally would touch the quarter sections at the crossing point ; and the idea was that the people should build their houses at the corner points, so that they could be together. My experience of the settlers of the North-west is that any one who attempted fatherly legislation of that kind would find himself disappointed, because the people will build their houses wherever they please, and not at any particular place because the government surveys the land in any particular way.
The -minister started to give us the names of those employed this year, but mentioned some exploring parties. Will those exploring parties be paid out of this fund ?
Yes, all exploring parties under the department are paid for out of these general votes.
Can the hon. minister give us the names of those who are going out this summer ?

We have not yet settled the list, and I could not make a definite statement. There are practically few changes in the men who go out. I may say that at the present time we are experiencing some difficulty in getting men of a high class, professionally speaking, to go on with the work of the department. One or two men have signified their willingness to go on at the present rate of pay. The fact is that operations of one kind and another are going on so rapidly that these men are offered higher pay than we are able to give them, and the surveyor general, with whom I have had some consultation on the matter, expresses some apprehension as to the position in which the department will he in this respect in two or three years. He is working on a plan to get young men into the service to be trained in the higher branches of the profession.
Miscellaneous-To supply seed grain to settlers whose crops were destroyed in 1900, to be secured by lien on land, $30,000.

The grain is being furnished only to new settlers and whom on account of the failure of crops last year have not the seed necessary for carrying on their operations. We are taking a lien for the amount of money, and the lien will be payable on or before the 1st of January next. That is, those who have not paid before will be expected to pay for it out of the next crop.
Is it a lien on the crop or on the land ?

On the land. Every person is required, before he can get seed grain under this vote, to make an affidavit that (1) he has made entry of a certain piece of land-describing it; (2) he has not been living on it and cultivating it longer than four years ; (3) he has so many acres prepared'for crop ; (4) he has not the necessary seed and no money to purchase the same ; (5) he agrees that the seed received from the government shall be sown on the land. We are endeavouring to hedge it around with safeguards. I think we are pretty sure to get our money back at the time arranged, unless there is a crop failure next season.
The department is having some experience in that line, what has been the result ?

I think we have put this in such a shape that the people will understand that it is not a permanent loan. They are told by our agents that if they get this money they will be expected to pay it back. A large Mr. SIFTON.
number of new settlers have gone in there and spent all the money they had. Last year the crop was a total failure, indeed for 25 years there had not been so great a disaster. I think it is good economy for the government to give them one chance at least.
Farther amount required for the cost of investigations, demarkations and other astroni-mical work of the Department of the Interior, $7,500.

The principal thing for which we require an additional expenditure above what we had anticipated, is the fact that we are arriving at an arrangement with the United States whereby we will go on and demark the boundary line between the United States and Canada in British Columbia and the North-west Territories, at certain points where the mounds have been destroyed. We are not going to have an actual treaty, because a treaty is not necessary, but we will have an amicable arrangement under which there will not be a new boundary formed. We are simply going to re-mark the boundary where it has already been fixed.
What surveyors have you engaged on that work ?

Mr. McCarthy and Mr. O'Hara have been assigned for that work. Mr. McCarthy is one of the oldest and very best officers of the department, and has had great experience as an explorer.
Amount, required to compensate Wm. Purdy for certain improvements of lots Nos. 75, 76 and 77 in the parish of St. Clement, $500.

That is to cover a case in which, owing to a mistake by the officers of the department at the head office, they sold lands on which a squatter had settled, and this is to compensate him in part for the improvements that he made upon the land.

While these items are going through, I would like to call the attention of the minister to a case that I brought to the attention of the department, but which probably did not come under his personal notice. Mr. R. J. Bull took up a homestead near Yorkton in 1882. In 1885 when the rebellion occurred, he turned out to assist in supressing the rebellion. I am not sure whether he became a volunteer or was teaming in supplies, but he contracted hip disease and has been disabled ever since. He has not received his homestead, which it appears to me he would be entitled to, because he lived there, not the whole three years, but a good deal over two years. But he performed his settlement duties for-, we will say, two years and a half, and perhaps more. But he did not comply strictly with the requirements of

the law, because he was prevented from doing so by having contracted a disease in the service of his country. Now, I see by the recent amendments to the Land Act that the government have provided for such cases, and I presume that it will be retroactive to this extent, that Mr. Bull, not having yet received his patent, could apply for his patent under that clause of the Land Act, and there are other conditions. But it is a case that, on its merits, I think would entitle Mr. Bull to the most generous consideration of the department. I am sure that it would be a compliance with the spirit of the law, it would be an act of justice to Mr. Bull, and certainly it could not be objected to by any one who is the most ardent stickler for complying with the letter of the regulations. I would ask the Minister of the Interior to give special consideration to Mr. Bull's claim. I left a letter regarding it with the department, but that letter has been returned to me. I would like it to receive the personal consideration of the minister, because I consider that these men who, in perilous times, have not hesitated to do their duty by their country, should receive justice at any rate. That is all that is required in the case of Mr. Bull.

I have so many cases of that kind coming before me that I cannot at present remember that this ease was one of them. I think I should probably have remembered it if it had been brought to my attention.
It was during the present session of parliament.

Then it has not been brought to my personal attention. Certainly if the claim was mentioned to me, the circumstances were not. If the fact be that this man took up a homestead, that he bona fide lived on it for two years, and then about that time went away and volunteered to serve the government in putting down the rebellion, and was injured in that service and incapacitated, I perfectly agree with my hon. friend that he ought to get his patent. My deputy informs me that the land is still available. I will look into the matter further and try to see that his claim is recognized.
Further amount required for salaries and expenses connected with the commission apointed to inquire into half-breed claims in the Northwest Territories, out of which payment be made to A. J. A. McKenna and N. 0. Cot6 as halfbreed commissioners, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act, $14,465.
I want to ask the hon. minister if the work of that commission is coming to a close ?

It will be finished in the early part of the 155
summer. Mr. McKenna is going out to finally close it up within a few weeks.
Indian Affairs-Ontario and Quebec-'fMedical attendance, $3,021.69.

The hon. Minister of the Interior promised to give some information in regard to matters on Walpole Island, to which I called the hon. gentleman's attention, as he will remember, some time ago. Perhaps he can give the information now.

My information in regard to the statement which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) made upon the discussion of the; main estimates, on the 10th of April, is to the effect that the information in the department is contrary to the statement of the hon. gentleman, that the Indians on Walpole Island have objected to the appointment of Dr. Hay. A petition was received from the Indians in March, 1897, asking for the appointment of Dr. Hay, and in compliance with their wishes that appointment was made. The information which the department has from the Indians goes to show that the Indians avail themselves of the services of the medical officer when they are in need of a physician. That is the information we have received, but if the hon. gentleman has reason to believe that a different state of affairs exists, I presume the only way it can be settled will be by sending an inspector up to make a special visit.

I do not propose to take the responsibility of making a statement that would warrant the hon. gentleman in taking that course. In regard to the petition, that was one that was got up by a number of white persons, of course, very naturally, on behalf of Dr. Hay. If an appointment were to be made nobody would look for anything other than a supporter of the government should receive the appointment. But, the hon. gentleman should remember that the attending physician, Dr. Mitchell, who had been attending the Indians for many years, was dismissed under what is called offensive partisanship.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Was not Dr. Mitchell the vice-president of the Conservative association ?

Quite so. That is quite an honourable position, and I have never heard that it was a crime.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
No.

It seems the hon. gentleman regarded this as a crime because he cut his head off.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
No, it was no crime at all.

It is a matter of notoriety that the Indians refused to avail themselves



of the services of Dr. Hay. I need hardly say anything to the hon. gentleman, who knows better than I do from his long experience of the Indian character, that they will refuse to employ persons with whom they are not acquainted, even though they may be infinitely better. I have never discussed the matter with the agent, Mr. Mc-Kelvie, but a Methodist minister by the name of Rev. Mr. Pickard called my attention to it.
Is he a missionary on the reserve ?

Yes, he is the missionary of the Methodist Church. He called my attention to the fact that the Indians were dying in large numbers, and he made the request that I should write to the department. I did not do so, but I suggested that the better way would be for him to write to the department and state matters as he found them. I think my hon. friend is not quite right in stating that there has been no communication received by the department. The hon. acting Minister of the Interior, during the minister's absence, stated in this House last year, in answer to some inquiries made during the time the estimates were going through, that he had received a letter from Mr. Pickard on the subject. That letter must be in the department, and I think the hon. gentleman is not possessed this evening of the information bearing on the subject, as Mr. Pickard told me he had written to the department, and the hon. acting minister stated last year that he had received such a communication. Of course, that was not read, and I do not know the contents of it. But, the matter was thought of suflicient importance by Mr. Pickard to call the attention of the department to it. Mr. Pickard did not do it for the purpose of favouring any political friends, or to put Dr. Hay at a disadvantage, because Mr. Pickard is a warm supporter of the present government, and whatever he may have stated was entirely without any party colouring. I call the hon. gentleman's attention to it for the reason that in dismissing Dr. Mitchell without cause the department have not only done an injustice to him, but this action has been followed by serious results, because the Indians fail to employ Dr. Hay to a very great extent.
Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the acting minister last year said he had received a letter ?
Yes.

I will have the ' Hansard' looked up and 1 will call his attention to it and see if such a letter has been received. When my hon. friend spoke upon this subject before I had a copy of his remarks made and sent to the officers of the department, and they have Mr. CLANCY.
provided me with a written statement to the effect that no communication has been received on the subject from the missionary on the reserve-that is, Mr. Pickard, I presume-and that the information from the agent was, that the Indians are availing themselves of Dr. Hay's services. It is simply a question of fact, and we will have to investigate it and see what the facts are. In order to avoid unnecessary expense, I will instruct the inspector on his next trip to that part of the country to make a special report, to see Mr. Pickard, and to get a statement from him in regard to it.

The hon. gentleman will not get the information by referring to ' Hansard ' of last year. The question was asked across the floor of the House, and the hon. acting Minister of the Interior stated that he was not quite sure what the facts were, but that he would look them up. He came over to my seat an evening or two afterwards and stated that he had such a communication. It would not appear in ' Hansard.'

I will see that the inspector calls upon Mr. Pickard upon his next trip to that part of the country.
Indians, N.B., $2,000.
Could not these items be put in the main estimates quite as well as here ?

The Indian estimates are invariably prepared in the latter part of November, and they are considered by council in December and January. In this case, owing to the severity of the winter, there were more demands than usual on the department for medical assistance, and the officers could not foresee that.
That might apply to medical assistance, but surely the necessity for seed grain could have been foreseen.
We have a great deal of trouble in connection with these little accounts for medical services. In some cases we have doctors on small salaries and there is continual complaint.
In Ontarto most of your medical men are engaged by the year at an annual salary.
That is the case when the Indians have a fund of their own, but in the maritime provinces they have no funds.
In the Manitoulin Island, for instance, the doctor gets a salary and he furnishes the drugs.
That is paid by the Indians out of their own funds.
Do the Indians employ the doctor ?
No. The department appoints all the officers whether they are paid out of the funds of the Indian band or not.
You have items here for Ontario as well as for the maritime provinces.

There are certain Indians in Ontario who have no funds of their own and this vote applies to them.
North-west Territories-Relief of Indians outside treaty limits, $5,000.

Last November reports came that the Indians at Oxford House, who are outside of the treaty limits, were suffering greatly and that some of them had starved to death. The Minister of the Interior stated that newspaper reports to that effect had reached his department, but that these reports were not confirmed. Apparently word of this has got to that part of the country, and I have been informed that there was a good deal of suffering last winter. I am told that relief was distributed by the Hudson Bay Company, and the cost refunded to the company by the government. There has been some dissatisfaction as to the manner in which this relief was applied, and I will ask that some further inquiry be made in this matter. My informant writes :
For some years back there has been a general falling off in the line of deer, rabbits, moose and beaver, which had hitherto been the support of the Indians as to food. Fish, too, have been failing in numbers. This has all been fully reported to the Indian Department.
Last winter, 1899-1900, was the hardest ever known in this country. Everywhere there was extremes of destitution. Oxford House, God's Lake, Island Lake, Front Lake, and in all the country tributary to these places there was starvation, nakedness and suffering of every kind. At Sandy Lake, tributary to Island Lake, nearly thirty people died of starvation. This I have from reliable witnesses. I have not as yet the details of these cases, but I am going there next June, and shall be particular to investigate the matter more thoroughly. Here, too, within ten miles of this house one man fell dead through sheer weakness after a long period of hunger. There was general distress, and at the same time the people were doing their best to provide for themselves.
Here and at God's Lake there has been some relief work done, but in no case has it been adequate to prevent suffering to almost extreme degrees, and the worst is yet to come. Supplies are now exhausted.
There is one point to which, I think, very grave exception should be taken, and that is the matter of relief is entirely in the hands of the Hudson's Bay Company, and they are certainly using the advantage to help those Indians who go to the bush for the winter, and those who desire to be near the missionary all winter are left to shift pretty much for themselves.
I am informed that there was some discrimination by the Hudson Bay Company 155}
against the Indians who remained at home during the winter and in favour of those who went to the bush. I am not, of course, familiar with the particulars, but I understand that some of the Indians prefer to remain in camp near the mission.
Most of them do.
I suppose these would be called lazy Indians, but at all events my informant states that they were not assisted as they ought to have been.

Would the hon. gentleman * (Mr. Brittbn) tell us who the writer of this letter is ? Is he a missionary ? There are times when there is a little friction between the missionaries and the Hudson Bay Company ; but my experience of twenty-two years in the country, is that the Hudson Bay . Company never allow the Indians to starve to death. In hard times they give the Indians assistance and take their chances on the hunt of the following year to enable the Indians to pay them.
All I ask is that inquiry should be made, because it is stated that starvation has taken place there, and that some of the Indians moved away to a point on Lake Winnipeg.

I think my hon. friend has perhaps stumbled on correct information, when he says that discrimination was made between the Indians who went out to work in winter and the Indians who stayed in camp. Probably the officers of the company refused assistance to those who refused to avail themselves of offers to earn money. However, that is a surmise. I may say to the committee that I have made no change in the system that has been pursued for years in the department. While it has its faults, it is probably the best that could be adopted for the purpose of meeting a very difficult set of circumstances. There is a vast tract of country in the remoter districts in which the government have no agents, and in which the expense of keeping agents for the purpose of affording relief in odd years when relief might bo required, would be enormous. It would amount to keeping up an immense establishment, and the cost of transporting supplies would he out of all reason. The government made this arrangement some years ago with the Hudson Bay Company. That company has its posts at nearly all these remote points, and it undertakes to see, as far as possible) that there is no actual starvation where it has supplies to prevent it. I want to say to my hon. friends that great care has to be exercised in dealing with the Indians, because if you create the impression in their minds that ail they have to do is to say they are hungry, to have food supplied to them, they will be foun^

at the Hudson Bay Company's posts every day in the year, and you will incur endless trouble. The Hudson Bay Company, who . have had a great deal of experience in dealing with Indians, have an understanding with the government that wherever they think there is a necessity, they give the Indians assistance, for which they send us a bill at the end of the year ; and the bills on their face show that care has been exercised, and that only what has been actually necessary has been done. For instance, one bill is for $118.93, another for -	$418.07, another for $108.50, and so on, the
total amount being $4,393.72. It is impossible for me to say anything at all as to the correctness of my hon. friend's information without making inquiry. There will be some difficulty in ascertaining whether there is any real foundation for the complaint or not, because it is not easy to get an exact statement of the facts, and the officers of the Hudson Bay Company will say that they exercised their discretion to the best of their ability. However, I will bring the matter to the attention of the Indian commissioner at Winnipeg, and if my hon. friend cares to give me, confidentially, a copy of that portion of the letter which contains the statement of facts, I will bring it to the attention of the Indian commissioner, and we will endeavour to get at the facts.
To provide for payment of allowance to J. A. Macrae when acting as half-breed and Indian commissioner for treaty No. 8, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $885.

During the last two or three years we have sent two or three members of the civil service away to the north of Edmonton on work connected with new treaties. The service is an important one, and we have paid them an extra allowance while they have been away. Mr. Macrae, who has been inspector of the department for many years, was sent up on that work last year, and this vote is to give him the same allowance as was given to the other commissioners.
What regular pay do you give him in addition to his regular salary ?

$5 a day and his expenses.

Has the hon. minister made any change in the regulations covering the inspection of meters used for electricity ? I have heard complaints that the owners of the electric meters are not allowed to have a representative present when these meters are being tested.

Amount required in connection with the office of warehouse commissioner and other expenditure connected with the inspection of grain, and to meet deficiency in inspection fees owing to short crop in Manitoba and North-west Territories, $7,000.

This is for all over Canada. Upon the recommendation of the royal commission which recently sat in Montreal, it is proposed to place inspectors and deputy Inspectors on salary and credit the fees to consolidated revenue. Should this system go into effect before the end of the fiscal year, an additional amount will be required to meet the expenditure. East of Port

Arthur it is expected that the expenditure *will be met by the fees collected. In Manitoba district, owing to the short crop last season, the receipts will not meet the expenditure to the end of June next, and a further amount is required.
What salaries are you paying the inspectors now ?

In Manitoba we are paying David Horn, chief inspector at Winnipeg, $4,000. We are paying F. E. Gibbs at Fort William $3,500, and an assistant inspector at $1,500. We are payiug the two assistant inspectors at Winnipeg $1,200 and $1,500 respectively.
Grain Commission, Montreal-Salaries, & c., $2,750.

Has that report
been brought down ?
Yes. It was laid before the House a month ago.
Has it been printed ?
I believe not.
Can the hon. minister give us in a few words the result of that investigation 7

Some complaints were made with regard to the inspection of grain in Montreal. The matter was taken up by Lord Strathcona, and the department was advised to hold an inquiry. Commissioners were appointed, Mr. Horn, of Winnipeg, Mr. Parmelee, the Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce, and Mr. Crane, of Montreal. The complaint was that the inspection had not been sufficiently thorough.
Yes.
There was some foundation for that complaint ?

The inspection was considered satisfactory to a certain extent; but there was only one inspector in Montreal, and the inspection was more in the hands of the shipper than [DOT]of independent parties.
